SUSTAINABLE MANAGEMENT OF SPRING WATER RESOURCES IN GUNUNG MEJA NATURAL TOURISM PARK, INDONESIA: BIOPHYSICAL INSIGHTS AND DEVELOPMENT SCENARIOS

Journal: Water Conservation and Management (WCM)
Author: Mahmud, Amalia Lakehu, Wahyudi, Febriza Dwiranti, Darma, Abdul Azis, Christian S. Imburi, David Mores Soindemi

ABSTRACT

Manokwari city, as the capital of West Papua Province, faces challenges in water availability and continuity. The aim of the research is to assess biophysical characteristics of springs (including spring type and the surrounding vegetation) and to develop scenarios of water management for sustainable water supplies. The research combined field survey using plot sampling methods to collect biophysical data and interview methods along with SWOT analysis to develop management scenario. The results show that six spring patterns were identified: springs coming from roots and rocks, springs emerging from rock seepages, springs from rock crevices, springs arising from caves, springs from gaps between rocks, and springs resulting from seepage in soil pores. The largest water discharge comes out spring between rocks, while the smallest discharge occurs from seepage in soil pores. Pometia pinnata, one of Papua endemic plant species, is the dominant vegetation and has the highest infiltration capacity and groundwater content. Water use includes for household consumption, district military uses and sold to the public. SWOT analysis suggests that the most effective water management scenarios can be implemented by nature resources conservation agency (BKSDA) in collaboration with regional water company (PDAM) and local youth group. The most effective scenario for the sustainable use of springs and broad benefits for community ultimately relies on the policies of central and regional government.
